title: Blue Report 2026: where defences really work, and where they only seem to
summary: The fourth annual Picus Security report: more than 338 million simulated attacks run in customers' real networks. The overall picture: the perimeter holds better (69% of attacks stopped), but inside the network, in logs and in alerts there are still plenty of blind spots.
body: Picus Security sells systems that safely imitate attacks on a company (the BAS class) and every year pulls together statistics on what those systems see at customers. Blue Report 2026 is the fourth such edition. The numbers come not from a lab but from working networks, so they show more honestly how security controls behave in real life.

The headline: of every three attacks, two are stopped, but only about one in seven produces an alert. Event logs are kept better (58%), yet turning them into a signal for a human rarely works. That makes a handy opening for a customer conversation: "You have logs, but does anyone check that the rules actually fire?"

New in 2026: for the first time the report measured what happens after an attacker is already inside. Here defences stop only 37% of actions. Loud steps (running programs, moving between computers) are blocked often, while quiet ones (mapping the network, reading stored passwords) meet almost no resistance.

The report is a vendor document, and Picus openly offers its own platform as the cure. So read it as a good map of problems, not as neutral research. Below are the report's eight findings in plain words, with ATT&CK techniques and the solution classes that address them.

caveats: The report was prepared by a vendor that sells attack simulation (BAS) systems, and it contains promotional sections. Take its conclusions with that in mind.
The data comes from simulations in Picus customers' networks, not from real incidents, and the sample is not random. It is a guide, not market-wide statistics.
The mapping to ATT&CK techniques and solution classes below is our editorial interpretation; an asterisk (*) next to an ID means the ID itself does not appear in the report.

findings.title: A strong perimeter, a soft interior
findings.text: Once inside the network, defences stop only 37% of attacker actions. Reconnaissance and data gathering (Discovery · Collection) are blocked in roughly 10% of cases, reading credentials from memory and the registry in 22%, while running programs and moving between computers are blocked far more often (about 90% for lateral movement). Quiet steps pass almost unopposed.

solutions.why: Automated pentesting shows which quiet steps inside the network get through at your company, which is how Picus arrived at the 37% figure.
Identity protection notices suspicious use of passwords and tickets once the attacker is already inside.
Watches behaviour on the computer, not just known programs, so it can spot quiet password reading.
Notices when an account suddenly browses things it has never opened, which is a sign of reconnaissance.
Decoy accounts and files catch whoever is quietly exploring the network, since an ordinary user would never go there.

findings.title: Stealth and "quiet" techniques are barely stopped
findings.text: The worst-blocked techniques are the ones that hide traces: disabling command history (T1562.003 in the source, T1690 in MITRE ATT&CK v20) at 1%, running malicious code through signed system programs (T1216) at 9%, forcing a downgrade of protocol or logging (T1562.010 in the source, T1689 in v20) at 16%, and holding a payload dormant until a real target is confirmed (T1480.001) at 17%. The Stealth tactic is one of only two where defences got worse (53% to 47%).

solutions.why: Looks at actions rather than a program's signature, so it can notice a signed system utility suddenly doing something odd, or someone wiping the command history.
Gathers logs in one place and flags when they suddenly go silent, which is exactly what attackers are after.
Safely plays these techniques against your defences and shows which ones go unnoticed.

findings.title: Threat groups and ransomware: protection against specific adversaries is weakening
findings.text: Nine of the ten worst-blocked threat groups got more effective against defences; for the Play ransomware only 13% of simulations were stopped (50% last year). The average for the ten worst ransomware families fell from roughly 44% to 32%. General hardening of endpoints has not carried over to ransomware attack chains.

solutions.why: Runs full scenarios of known groups and ransomware against your network and shows at which step the chain is not interrupted.
Tells you which groups and ransomware families take an interest in your industry, so you can test your defences against exactly those.
Stops encryption by behaviour (mass file changes) even when the specific ransomware family is new.
If encryption still happens, clean backups give you a chance to recover without paying a ransom.
An isolated immutable vault keeps the ransomware from reaching the copies too.

findings.title: Malware downloads: indicator-based protection is falling behind
findings.text: Malicious file download scenarios are blocked in 50% of cases (60% last year, 71% in 2024). Protection that looks for known indicators (IOCs) always lags behind new threats, so it needs reinforcing with behaviour checks. The report also notes a rollback on macOS: from 76% to 61%.

solutions.why: Opens a suspicious file in a safe environment and watches what it does, instead of matching it against a list of known threats.
Catches malicious behaviour on the computer itself; check that the agent is really installed on macOS as well, where the score dropped.

findings.title: There are logs, but no alerts
findings.text: The share of attacks that left a trace in logs is 58%, while only 14% trigger an alert. The report calls this a "detection engineering" problem. Of the causes of detection rule failures, 49% are performance issues (up from 24%): rules that are too broad, long time windows, slow queries. Another 41% are log collection issues, including "silent" ones where nobody ever sees the event.

solutions.why: This is where detection rules live; they need to be written for today's attacker behaviour and regularly checked to confirm they fire.
Adds behaviour analytics that turn scattered logs into a clear signal rather than yet another stream of events.
Shows exactly which detection rules stay silent when a simulated attack passes by.

findings.title: Data theft and covert contact with the attacker's server
findings.text: Data theft is the worst-blocked area for the fourth year running: 7% (3% in 2025). In other words, more than nine out of ten attempts succeed. Covert contact between the attacker and the command server gets through too: application layer protocol (T1071) is blocked in 16% of cases, data encoding (T1132) in 9%.

solutions.why: Looks at the content and direction of data leaving the company and stops what should not be going out.
Analyses network traffic and spots unusual outbound connections and hidden command channels.
Limits where connections from inside the network can go at all, and inspects outbound traffic.

findings.title: Legitimate accounts are the weak spot
findings.text: Valid Accounts (T1078), meaning stolen or weak passwords, is stopped in only 15% of cases. The report names password spraying, MFA fatigue and token theft. An attacker who logs in "legitimately" looks to most tools like an ordinary user.

solutions.why: A second factor stops a stolen password from being enough on its own; methods resistant to phishing and prompt fatigue work best.
Notices suspicious sign-ins and the use of tickets and tokens once the password is already in the wrong hands.
Limits what can be done even with a privileged account and keeps a record of actions.

findings.title: The worst-covered vulnerabilities and web applications
findings.text: The ten worst-blocked recent vulnerabilities (CVEs) are stopped in under 25% of cases; the worst only in 8%. This is everyday software: a browser, archivers, a text editor, core OS components, crypto libraries. Web application protection (WAF) stops 61% (63% last year), which, in the authors' words, points to a plateau in tuning and input validation testing.

solutions.why: Shows where these vulnerabilities remain unpatched in your network so you can update them first.
IPS signatures temporarily cover a vulnerability when patching immediately is impossible, but they need testing against current CVEs.
Helps stop privilege escalation on the computer itself even if the vulnerability is not yet patched.
Filters malicious requests to a web application, but needs regular tuning or results stagnate.
Scans the web application from outside, like an attacker, and finds holes the WAF may have missed.
